At Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, there are discrepancies both above Shealtiel and below Zerubbabel. This is also the point where Matthew departs from the Old Testament record. In the Old Testament, Zerubbabel was a hero who led the Jews back from Babylon around 520 BC, governed Judah, and rebuilt the temple. Several times he is called a son of Shealtiel. He appears once in the genealogies in the Book of Chronicles, where his descendants are traced for several generations, but the passage has a number of peculiarities.

In time series forecasting, one common method to evaluate the accuracy of a forecasting model is to remove the last observation from the data, build a forecasting model using the remaining data, and then compare the forecast to the removed observation. This process is repeated for each observation in the data set, and the forecast accuracy is computed over all errors. This procedure is sometimes known as a "rolling forecasting origin" because the "origin" (k+i -1) at which the forecast is based rolls forward in time. Further, two-step-ahead or in general p-step-ahead forecasts can be computed by first creating a model using the initial k observations, then generating forecasts for the k+1, k+2, ..., k+p observations.

For time series data, the training set can only include observations prior to the test set. Therefore, no future observations can be used in constructing the forecast. Suppose k observations are needed to produce a reliable forecast; then the process works as follows: Starting with i=1, select the observation k + i for the test set, and use the remaining k-1 observations to estimate the forecasting model. Compute the error on the forecast for k+i. Repeat the above step for i = 2,...,T-k where T is the total number of observations. Compute the forecast accuracy over all errors. This makes efficient use of the available data, as only one observation is omitted at each step.
